1.content: Build native desktop apps that link the QuickGUI crate with Cargo. These guides use Rust. Choose Go or TypeScript in the sidebar for those language bindings. Rust apps link the quickgui crate into the executable. The CLI runs Cargo, packages the binary, and does not bundle libquickgui_host . Ordinary edits rebuild the selected crate; there is no FFI host library to reuse.
1.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu getting-started

2.content: A current stable Rust toolchain (1.90 or newer) Bun 1.3 or newer Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS ( xcode-select --install ) The first development build compiles wgpu and takes longer. Later edits reuse incremental Cargo artifacts.

3.content: Run the command below and choose Rust when prompted. bun run dev compiles the crate, packages and launches the app, and rebuilds on source changes. Pass --language rust to skip the language prompt.

4.content: The generated src/main.rs constructs an Application , opens a window, and implements View . Store state on the view and call cx.invalidate() after mutations.

5.content: check , test , and fmt dispatch to Cargo. Production builds compile with --release and write packaged apps under dist/ . Rust apps ship quickgui.json next to the executable (or in Contents/Resources on macOS) instead of a host shared library.

6.content: Explore the component reference , native services , and SwiftUI controls . The checkout includes examples/base_ui_components.rs and related examples/*.rs galleries.

7.content: Configure Rust projects, Cargo features, and native packaging. A QuickGUI Rust project keeps application code in a Cargo package and development commands in a small Bun package.
7.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu project-structure

8.content: The CLI generates these files. Commit Cargo.lock after the first successful build.

9.content: src/main.rs starts Application::new().run(...) and opens windows from that callback. Each window owns a View . entry in the config is the crate directory (or a Cargo.toml path). Split larger applications into ordinary Rust modules.

10.content: TOML supports the same keys. The CLI checks quickgui.toml before quickgui.config.ts . Rust apps must not set extensions , native.tags , or native.libraryPath ; enable crate features in Cargo.toml instead.

11.content: Applications depend on the quickgui crate. @quickgui/cli is a development dependency. Optional terminal and updater capabilities are Cargo features on quickgui , not separately bundled host libraries.

12.content: Use a shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR if you work on several Rust apps. The first wgpu build is slow; later incremental compiles reuse that target directory.

13.content: Enable the updater crate feature and check signed update manifests. Enable the updater feature on the quickgui crate. Rust apps do not load @quickgui/extension-updater ; they call UpdateClient in-process.
13.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu updater

14.content: Generate an Ed25519 key pair, then copy the public key into the project: Keep the private quickgui-update.key outside version control. Do not set extensions . Enable the crate feature: The CLI embeds the public key, application version, identifier, and feed URL in packaged metadata. A darwin-arm64 build checks https://downloads.example.com/my-app/appcast-darwin-arm64.xml unless updates.feedUrl overrides it.

15.content: Construct one UpdateClient after the application starts, outside View::render , so every window shares the session: A Check for Updates action can call check from a listener and cx.invalidate() when UI state should show progress.

16.content: Keep the client for the process lifetime. Closing a window must not drop it if other windows still need update status. Cooperative cancellation uses UpdateCancellation around download and staging.

17.content: macOS can also emit Sparkle appcasts when updates.publicKey is set. Windows and Linux use the signed JSON updater. Development builds should point at a disposable feed.

18.content: Signing needs the Minisign secret key in updates.minisignSecretKey or QUICKGUI_MINISIGN_SECRET_KEY . The private key is never embedded in the application.

19.content: Packaged Rust apps include the executable and quickgui.json . The updater client reads the embedded public key and current version from that metadata when you pass the values from AppInfo .

20.content: Share Rust modules in-app, or author native extensions for Go and TypeScript. A Rust application can share ordinary modules, or it can author a native extension that Go and TypeScript apps load. Rust apps themselves do not set extensions in quickgui.config.ts ; they enable crate features and depend on crates.
20.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu extensions

21.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Choose an extension type
21.content: What you are adding What you ship Core changes Components or application logic A Rust module or crate None Optional QuickGUI capabilities Cargo features such as updater and terminal None A native service for Go or TypeScript A cdylib , manifest, and typed wrapper None Native extensions run in the consumer's process. A Rust app already is that process: it links quickgui and does not load libquickgui_host .

22.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Create an extension project
22.content: Use this when Go or TypeScript apps should consume a native service. Extension scaffolds use the shared extension ABI. --npm-package sets the artifact package name.

23.content: Share UI by exporting functions that return Element : Return notice("Saved") as a child. Keep application-wide services outside View::render .

24.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Lay out a native extension
24.content: A native extension ships quickgui.extension.json , a versioned shared library, and declared resources. Its manifest identifies the service name, ABI, npm package, release version, library, and per-platform resources. Rust extensions can vendor extension_api.rs and build a cdylib without linking the renderer.

25.content: Rust applications enable features in Cargo.toml . They must not set top-level extensions : Go and TypeScript consumers declare the extension package in their own config. Custom extensions may use a scoped package such as @acme/extension-echo .

26.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Implement the native contract
26.content: Implement the bounded ServiceApi contract in the extension. Copy borrowed input before returning, keep event streams scoped to their sessions, and release worker resources when the session stops.

27.content: Go and TypeScript CLIs resolve and bundle declared extensions. A Rust app has nothing to register: Cargo links the crates you depend on. Optional renderer backends stay behind Cargo features.

28.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Build and package artifacts
28.content: App edits rebuild the selected crate. Rebuild an extension when its native implementation changes, then rebuild the consuming Go or TypeScript application to stage those bytes.

29.content: Test against a packed extension and CLI in a fresh Go or TypeScript project. Extension commands are asynchronous and share the bounded native event transport.

30.content: Manage windows, menus, dialogs, clipboard, and asynchronous native work. Call Application::new().run(...) once from main . Its startup callback creates windows and registers application services. Listeners run on the native UI thread.
30.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu native-services

31.content: cx.open_window(WindowOptions::new("Title").size(width, height), view) creates a window with its own View and retained tree. Closing the window drops that view. Handle macOS Dock reopening from Application::on_reopen when has_visible_windows is false.

32.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Commands and services
32.content: Typed APIs cover dialogs, clipboard, shell, appearance, menus, displays, and other platform services. Capture cx.window_handle() during a listener when later work needs that window.

33.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Events and file watching
33.content: Window events include focus, resize, appearance, minimize, fullscreen, and close. Application callbacks include reopen, activation, quit, and open URLs. Prefer native notifications over polling. Enable the file-watcher crate feature when you need filesystem events, and drop watchers with the owning view.

34.content: Store view state, invalidate on change, and rebuild only the declared tree. Store state on the View . render reads that state to build elements. Call cx.invalidate() after a mutation so the window schedules another render. The native core still retains layout, paint, and accessibility between frames.
34.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu reactivity

35.content: Keep fields on the view struct. Register listeners with cx.listener so activations can mutate those fields. A value you copy in render is the current frame's snapshot.

36.content: Compute derived values in render from the fields you already store. Keep derivations pure; perform writes from listeners. Store an expensive derivation on the view when several children need the same value in one frame.

37.content: Rust views do not subscribe with Go/TypeScript-style effects. Start external work from listeners or Application callbacks, and drop that work when the view is dropped. Window close releases the view and its listeners.

38.content: Calling cx.invalidate() marks the window dirty. Multiple invalidations in one event coalesce into one render. Do not install a frame loop for ordinary state updates; the window sleeps while it is clean.

39.content: Understand View::render, keyed identity, window ownership, and testing. View::render builds an element tree after invalidation or OS damage. Native layout, painting, focus, input, and accessibility remain in the core. Stable Element::id values preserve identity across renders.
39.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu rendering

40.content: Return impl IntoElement from render . Fluent builders construct retained elements. The window sleeps until invalidate or platform damage. Do not rebuild from a timer when nothing changed.

41.content: Omitting a branch drops its nodes. Sibling elements with stable ids keep their identities.

42.content: Give stateful rows stable id s. Use VirtualList or TableState for large collections and only mount visible rows.

43.content: Each open_window owns an independent view. Closing a child window must not drop its siblings. Handle macOS Dock reopening by constructing a fresh window when has_visible_windows is false.

44.content: ViewContext and EventContext expose the current WindowHandle during render and event dispatch.

45.content: examples/base_ui_components.rs is the broad UI gallery. Enable the inspector crate feature for the in-app inspector. Native integration checks are separate from cargo test .

46.content: Compose the complete QuickGUI component families with Rust builders. Implement View for application components. Primitives are functions that return Element . Compound components are copyable descriptors whose *_part methods decorate caller-owned elements.
46.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu components

47.content: Child views can also be functions that return Element when they have no retained state.

48.content: div , text , button , text_input , text_area , Markdown , img , svg , custom_shader , VirtualList , and optional Terminal are native building blocks. submit_button submits the nearest form .

49.content: Compound roots coordinate named parts through ids and state you store on the view. Keep parts under the intended root so focus and value relationships stay explicit.

50.content: Store values on the view and pass them into constructors such as Checkbox::new , SliderState , or text_input . Update those fields from listeners, then invalidate . There is no separate defaultValue layer: the view owns the state.

51.content: The reference covers selection controls, tabs, disclosure, fields, menus, context menus, pickers, dialogs, popovers, preview cards, drawers, navigation menus, ranges, splitters, progress, meters, toggles, toolbars, toasts, calendars, date/time fields, scroll areas, tables, trees, and SwiftUI controls. Run examples/base_ui_components.rs for a gallery.

52.content: Apply fluent style methods to each visual part. Parts remain unstyled so layout and colors belong to the application. State types such as SliderState , TabsState , SelectState , and ScrollAreaState expose the current native state for custom presentation.

53.content: Match nested native layouts with Rust-owned route matching and history. Router owns route matching, normalized locations, and bounded memory history. The view chooses which elements to mount from the current match.
53.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu routing

54.content: RouteDefinition::layout declares a pathless ancestor. Relative child paths join their parent; an absolute child path starts at the root.

55.content: Match the route chain and wrap inner content with layout elements. Pathless layouts appear in matched ancestry without adding a URL segment.

56.content: The controller supports push , replace , back , and forward . Navigation stays in the native application.

57.content: Query pairs are retained as bounded lists on RouteLocation .

58.content: Apply layout, typography, paint, and interaction styles to native elements. Fluent methods set layout, paint, typography, and interaction styles. Numeric lengths are logical pixels.
58.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu styling

59.content: Fixed presets such as flex_col , p_3 , rounded_lg , and text_lg match the helpers generated for Go and TypeScript. p_3 is 12 pixels on the four-pixel spacing scale. For custom values, use rounded(10.0) , p(14.0) , and w / h .

61.content: Write functions that take and return Element :

62.content: Use flex , flex_col , flex_grow , alignment, and gap . Set min_w(0.0) or min_h(0.0) on flexible scroll containers so content can shrink.

63.content: Use grid plus track, placement, and span methods for two-dimensional layouts. Grid sizing is native; children keep ids when positions change.

64.content: Font family, weight, size, wrapping, and selection use retained native text. Colors accept Color::rgb8 , Color::rgba8 , and packed linear values. Images and SVGs share the core’s bounded caches.

66.hierarchy: Styling & Layout › Groups and named group hover
66.content: Use a named group on an ancestor and group_hover on descendants to style coordinated states. The core resolves group membership and invalidates the affected retained subtree.

67.content: Use native transitions and animated images without a frame-polling loop. Native transitions interpolate paint-only style changes while the element stays mounted.
67.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu animations

69.content: Change a style field from view state and call invalidate . The core interpolates supported transitions. Do not reconstruct the view on each frame.

70.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Timing and frame rate
70.content: Transition::new takes a Duration . Set easing with with_easing and cap cadence with max_fps while animation is active. That ceiling is not an idle scheduling source.

71.content: TransitionProperties covers background, border color and width, radius, text color, box shadow, opacity, and transform. Layout lengths stay declaration-time values because they require Taffy.

72.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Mounting and reduced motion
72.content: Keep an overlay mounted for its exit transition when the component supports that lifecycle. Respect the platform reduced-motion preference instead of imposing a frame loop.

73.content: img uses native image resources, including animated GIF/WebP sources. The core owns playback deadlines, cache limits, and visibility-based suspension; loading a static image does not request idle frames.

74.content: Build controlled text inputs, fields, choices, and pickers. Text controls are controlled: pass the current value into text_input / text_area and write edits from on_input .
74.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu forms-and-input

76.content: Field and Fieldset declare accessible relationships among labels, descriptions, controls, and errors. Validation mode and debounce deadlines live on FieldState .

77.content: Compose Checkbox , CheckboxGroup , RadioGroup , Radio , and Switch with their indicators and labels. Store checked values on the view and update them from listeners.

78.content: SelectState , ComboboxState , and AutocompleteState declare options ahead of native filtering and keyboard navigation. Keep option values stable.

79.content: Input listeners receive the next text. Pointer, key, gesture, drop, and submit handlers are registered on ViewContext . Use declared listeners so the core knows which events the view observes.

80.content: Compose popovers, dialogs, native panels, and file dialogs. In-window overlays stay in the retained scene. Operating-system dialogs use platform prompts.
80.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu overlays-and-dialogs

81.content: Compose Popover trigger, positioner, popup, and arrow parts. The core owns placement, collisions, focus, outside interaction, and dismissal. Store open on the view.

82.content: Dialog::new and Dialog::alert add modal semantics plus title, description, backdrop, viewport, and close parts. Restore focus through restore_focus_to ; do not install a second focus trap.

83.content: SystemPopover owns a separate native panel anchored to a mounted node. It can cross the parent’s content bounds and is disposed with its owner.

85.content: Embed real SwiftUI controls inside the retained QuickGUI renderer. Enable the swift-ui crate feature. Hosted controls are AppKit/SwiftUI views composed with QuickGUI’s retained scene, not replicas painted by wgpu.
85.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu swift-ui

86.content: Construct MacSwiftUiHost , sync a descriptor tree, and mount the NSView with native_view .

87.content: The host includes buttons, toggles, sliders, steppers, progress views, gauges, text and secure fields, pickers, segmented controls, date/color pickers, and popovers. Each component’s reference lists its builder methods.

89.content: MacSwiftUiHost::fitting_size reports intrinsic native sizing. Keep the parent’s dimensions constrained so native measurement and GPU layout agree.

90.content: SwiftUI hosting is macOS-specific. System availability determines optional appearances, including Liquid Glass. Go and TypeScript expose the same core capability through their adapters.

91.content: Style native controls and host QuickGUI content inside SwiftUI. Apply SwiftUiModifier values in declaration order. Convenience builders such as style , control_size , and disabled append those modifiers.
91.keywords: rust cargo crate view wgpu swift-ui-hosting

92.content: Button style, border shape, control size, label style, tint, and disabled state are supported. Apply them on the descriptor before sync .

93.content: The operating system draws native glass where available. Layout and hit testing remain owned by the native hosting layer.

94.content: Embed a QuickGUI subtree back into the SwiftUI tree with SwiftUiQuickGuiHost and MacSwiftUiHost::set_embedded_view . The hosted surface is an ordinary QuickGUI renderer.

95.content: SwiftUiPopover has explicit trigger and content element lists. A SwiftUiQuickGuiHost inside that content owns a separate ordinary QuickGUI renderer.

96.content: Native and Rust ownership must agree: an embedded renderer is disposed with its host, and a presented panel is disposed with its owner. Dropping MacSwiftUiHost releases the NSHostingView.

A host that renders many declared trees through one view passes an accessor that captures which [`TreeState`] each registered listener resolves.

Checkbox pub fn new(state: impl Into<ToggleState>) -> Self parent pub fn parent(children: impl IntoIterator<Item = bool>) -> Self Derive a parent checkbox from the checked values of the boxes it governs. This is Base UI's `parent` checkbox: every child checked reports on, none reports off, and a mix reports mixed. QuickGUI keeps no child registry — the application passes the values it is already rendering — so the derivation stays a pure function of the caller's own data. ``` use quickgui::{Checkbox, ToggleState}; assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, true]).state(), ToggleState::On); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([false, false]).state(), ToggleState::Off); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, false]).state(), ToggleState::Mixed); // An empty group is unchecked rather than mixed. assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([]).state(), ToggleState::Off); ``` read_only pub const fn read_only(mut self, read_only: bool) -> Self Show a value the user may read but not change, Base UI's `readOnly`. Unlike a disabled checkbox, a read-only one stays focusable and stays in the Tab sequence. QuickGUI projects the state and refuses the transition through [`Self::next_state`]; the application's own listener asks for that transition rather than toggling blindly. state pub const fn state(self) -> ToggleState Configures state for this part. is_read_only pub const fn is_read_only(self) -> bool Configures is read only for this part. next_state pub const fn next_state(self) -> Option<ToggleState> The state an activation moves this checkbox to, or `None` when it refuses. Mixed and off both move to on, and on moves to off, which is the web's tri-state contract. A read-only checkbox returns `None`, so a click listener that asks before writing cannot change a value the control is refusing. parent_next_checked pub const fn parent_next_checked(self) -> Option<bool> The checked value activating a parent checkbox moves its whole group to. A partially or fully unchecked parent checks everything; a fully checked one clears it. Returns `None` when the parent is read-only. Rust applications enable features in Cargo.toml . They must not set top-level extensions : Go and TypeScript consumers declare the extension package in their own config. Custom extensions may use a scoped package such as @acme/extension-echo .

Rust views do not subscribe with Go/TypeScript-style effects. Start external work from listeners or Application callbacks, and drop that work when the view is dropped. Window close releases the view and its listeners.

src/main.rs starts Application::new().run(...) and opens windows from that callback. Each window owns a View . entry in the config is the crate directory (or a Cargo.toml path). Split larger applications into ordinary Rust modules.

Store values on the view and pass them into constructors such as Checkbox::new , SliderState , or text_input . Update those fields from listeners, then invalidate . There is no separate defaultValue layer: the view owns the state.

Store view state, invalidate on change, and rebuild only the declared tree. Store state on the View . render reads that state to build elements. Call cx.invalidate() after a mutation so the window schedules another render. The native core still retains layout, paint, and accessibility between frames.

Understand View::render, keyed identity, window ownership, and testing. View::render builds an element tree after invalidation or OS damage. Native layout, painting, focus, input, and accessibility remain in the core. Stable Element::id values preserve identity across renders.
Use a named group on an ancestor and group_hover on descendants to style coordinated states. The core resolves group membership and invalidates the affected retained subtree.
Use a shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR if you work on several Rust apps. The first wgpu build is slow; later incremental compiles reuse that target directory.
Use flex , flex_col , flex_grow , alignment, and gap . Set min_w(0.0) or min_h(0.0) on flexible scroll containers so content can shrink.
Use grid plus track, placement, and span methods for two-dimensional layouts. Grid sizing is native; children keep ids when positions change.
Use native transitions and animated images without a frame-polling loop. Native transitions interpolate paint-only style changes while the element stays mounted.
Use this when Go or TypeScript apps should consume a native service. Extension scaffolds use the shared extension ABI. --npm-package sets the artifact package name.
ViewContext and EventContext expose the current WindowHandle during render and event dispatch.
